JMPR: Sum of pyrasulfotole and desmethyl-pyrasulfotole and its conjugates, expressed as pyrasulfotole.
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Pyrasulfotole
efsa_comments:
The active substance has never been assessed at EU level. The EU residue definitions for enforcement was established in 2008, when the a.s. was included in Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 (MRLs above the LOQ set for oats, liver and kidney of bovine). The proposed residue definitions are based on metabolism studies with wheat, rotational crops and livestock.
In cereals, pyrasulfotole was extensively metabolised and not detected in grains; pyrasulfotole-benzoic acid (MTFM-BA) was the main compound (24–98% TRR) in all wheat matrices (forage, hay, straw and grains). Glucose conjugates of desmethyl-pyrasulfotole were identified in wheat forage, hay and straw; desmethyl-pyrasulfotole was predominant residue in field trials.
MTFM-BA was identified as the only metabolite in rotational crops > 0.01 mg/kg (it is a common soil metabolite of isoxaflutole, but DT50 for this metabolite varied between studies). It is noted that the residue definition in plant commodities shall be restricted to cereals only. In livestock metabolism, pyrasulfotole was the predominant compound in animal matrices, milk and eggs; desmethyl- pyrasulfotole was the major metabolite identified in milk (12% TRR).
Livestock feeding studies were available in lactating cows (pyrasulfotole) and laying hens (MTFM-BA). On the basis that MTFM-BA is a common metabolite with isoxaflutole and that it is a (minor) rat metabolite and of no toxicological concern according to toxicity studies, it was not included in the residue definitions for plant and animal matrices. The metabolite is also the main compound the livestock is exposed to.
Validated analytical enforcement methods are available to control residues of pyrasulfotole, desmethyl-pyrasulfotole (free and conjugated) and MTFM-BA in plant and animal matrices. The method involves hydrolysis step to release conjugates. The storage stability of desmethyl-pyrasulfotole is limited to 3 months in high water content commodities (relevant for forage) and dry feed.

efsa_comments:
It is noted that in the context of the recent MRL review under Art. 12 of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 (EFSA, 2023e), EFSA proposed the following residue definitions applicable for plant and animal products:
RD enf: dithiocarbamates (dithiocarbamates determined and expressed as CS2, including maneb, mancozeb, metiram, propineb, thiram and ziram)
RD RA: (1) mancozeb (analysed as CS2 and expressed as mancozeb)
RD RA: (2) ETU
For enforcement purposes the EU and JMPR residue definitions are comparable. To express the residues of mancozeb as CS2, the molecular weight conversion factor of 1.78 is applicable.
For risk assessment purposes the residue definitions differ as the RD set by the JMPR includes metabolite ETU, which, according to the JMPR assessment, is 7.5 times more toxic than parent compound. Therefore, to express residues of ETU as mancozeb toxicity equivalents the ratio of the ADIs of mancozeb and ETU (7.5) is used by the JMPR.
In the EU, ETU is included in a separate residue definition, to be assessed against the TRV derived for ETU.

efsa_comments:
The residue definition for enforcement derived by JMPR and EFSA are the same. For risk assessment, residue definitions are the same except for root/tuber crops for which EFSA proposed including SYN 500003.
Since data were not sufficient to conclude on the toxicological profile of SYN 500003, a risk management decision was taken in the framework of the MRL review to add a footnote requesting additional toxicological studies was added to the MRLs established for onions and spring onions. Erroneously, this footnote was also included for tomatoes and courgettes, but not for other root and tuber vegetables (potatoes, beetroots and radishes). The point will be addressed in a new regulation currently under discussion in the PAFF meeting.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Sulfoxaflor (sum of isomers)
Peer review (EFSA, 2014d):
Sulfoxaflor
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor.
At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474. X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items.
The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014d). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products was provisional. Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound.
The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

JMPR: Sulfoxaflor
EU:
Peer review (EFSA, 2014d):
Sum of parent sulfoxaflor and metabolite X11719474, expressed as sulfoxaflor
If metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for risk assessment will become parent sulfoxaflor only.
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor.
At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474. X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items.
The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014d). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products was provisional. Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound.
The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

efsa_comments:

1) Flupyradifurone
2) Difluoroacetic acid (DFA)
Peer review (EFSA, 2015b):
1) Flupyradifurone
2) Difluoroacetic acid (DFA) (expressed as DFA)
efsa_comments:
In the EU, a separate enforcement residue definition for plant and animal commodities is set that refers to a soil metabolite difluoroacetic acid (DFA, expressed as DFA). Thus, the EU and JMPR residue definitions are not compatible.
The risk assessment residue definition derived by the JMPR for plant commodities is wider as it includes also 6‐CNA metabolite, which was not proposed to be included in the EU residue definition by the pesticides peer review. Thus, the exposure calculated for this residue definition of JMPR would be overestimated to a certain extent. 6‐CNA is minor metabolite which is a common metabolite with other a.s. (e.g. imidacloprid).
The risk assessment residue definitions for animal commodities set in the EU and by JMPR are comparable.

efsa_comments:
In 2017, the EU submitted a concern form regarding the residue definition, because quinclorac methyl ester which is 10 times more toxic than quinclorac was not included in the residue definition for enforcement, noting that quinclorac methyl might be used as a variant of the a.s. quinclorac in plant protection products (to be confirmed by the manufacturer of the a.s.).
The EU concern was addressed by JMPR in 2018: JMPR confirmed the previously derived residue definition, highlighting that the overall exposure was low.
The EU reserved its position to include quinclorac methyl ester in the EU residue definition for enforcement for rapeseed, considering the higher toxicity of the methyl ester.
EFSA still has concerns that the RD for enforcement does not cover the more toxic variant quinclorac methyl ester, but acknowledges that the inclusion of a variant for which no data were submitted to JMPR is not in line with the JMPR assessment practice.

judgment_basis_ko: JMPR Enforcement는 enol을 추가하고 EU 현행 법규는 spiromesifen만이다. 해설이 현행 법규와 아직 반영되지 않은 enol 제안을 구분한다.
classification_stage: 기존8개 + 정의 미설정·미확정 / 원문 해석·판단 근거 부족 = 총10개; 원본 라벨·기존 검토 상태 유지
JMPR:
Sum of spiromesifen and spiromesifen‐enol, expressed as spiromesifen
The residue is fat soluble
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Spiromesifen
MRL review (EFSA, 2019a): Inconclusive (No residue definition proposed in the absence of appropriate metabolism studies)
Peer review (EFSA, 2012f): Not proposed
The residue is not fat soluble
efsa_comments:
The current residue definitions for enforcement established in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 are not directly comparable with the residue definition proposed by JMPR which comprises also the enol‐metabolite. In the framework of the MRL review, the enol‐metabolite was proposed to be included in the residue definition for enforcement, but recommendations of this assessment have not yet been legally implemented.
As regards the risk assessment residue definition (RD‐RA), for plants, JMPR proposed to include not only the enol‐metabolite but also 4‐hydroxymethyl‐Sp‐enol, free and conjugated; the latter was not proposed by the peer review. In the framework of the Article 12 MRL review, two RD‐RA were proposed: (1) primary crops, except leafy crops including spiromesifen‐enol (M01) and (2) for leafy and rotational crops, also including enol (M01), spiromesifen‐4‐hydroxymethyl (M02) and its conjugate M03. It was noted that the inclusion of metabolites M04 and M06 in the residue definition for rotational leafy crops may need to be reconsidered, based on the outcome of a rotational field trial on succeeding leafy (EFSA, 2019a).
Since the proposed Codex MRLs are for fruits and pulses and oilseeds only, for which the RD‐RA is the same in the EU and JMPR, the difference in the RD‐RA derived by JMPR and the EU (for leafy crops and rotational crops) will not have an impact on the assessment.
It is noted that for animal products, residue definitions at the EU level could not be proposed in the absence of appropriate metabolism studies. There are no Codex MRL proposals for livestock commodities.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Afidopyropen (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
No EU peer review and no MRL review
efsa_comments:
Plant products: In metabolism studies, parent afidopyropen was the major compound in the majority of primary crop commodities (up to 61% TRR). However, in soya bean, parent afidopyropen was detected at very low concentrations in dry soya bean seed (0.4% TRR, 0.001 mg/kg). The metabolite trigonelline (M031) identified in soya bean seeds (47% TRR) is also a naturally occurring alkaloid in many plants. The dimer M007 was found in dry soya bean seeds at 1% TRR and 12% TRR, depending on the study.
Animal products: Parent afidopyropen was the major compound in animal tissues, ranging from 17% TRR in goat kidney to 97% TRR in egg yolk and up to 6.8% TRR in milk. The ester cleavage metabolite M001 was a major metabolite in milk, liver, kidney and muscle, ranging from 24% to 66% TRR, and was also a minor metabolite in fat (4.6% TRR). M017 was a major metabolite in hen liver. The metabolic pathways in goat and hens are similar to that which is reported in rat.
CPCA is a metabolite that is formed by cleavage of the cyclopropane carboxylic acid ester moieties from the parent molecule. Parent afidopyropen contains two CPCA groups. From livestock and rat metabolism studies it is known that metabolism can lead to the cleavage of only one or both CPCA ester moieties. Including CPCA in the residue definition (expressed as parent compound) seems problematic, since one molecule of afidopyropen may generate 1 or 2 molecules of CPCA. Hence the molecular weight conversion factor to recalculate the amount of CPCA to afidopyropen equivalents could be either 6.9 or 3.45. Hence, this leads to ambiguous results.
In 2021 CCPR, the EU expressed concerns on the appropriateness of the risk assessment residue definitions derived by JMPR, as the inclusion of CPCA in the residue definition for risk assessment may lead to ambiguous results.
According to the results of the livestock metabolism and feeding studies, parent compound was below the LOQ while the levels of the total residues (parent +M001 + CPCA‐carnitine expressed as parent) was more than 20 times higher. Hence, parent compound is considered not a valid marker substance and therefore the RD for enforcement should be reconsidered for muscle/meat and milk.

efsa_comments:
JMPR identified the following information missing that would be desirable to derive proposals for enforcement residue definitions for plant and animal products:
Submission of the metabolism data in alfalfa
Identification of major unknown components in all plant matrices from broccoli, maize and peanut metabolism studies
In the EU assessment the RMS suggested in the RAR with respect to the non‐identified metabolites that these metabolites of higher polarity are not relevant since they are intermediates in of the natural detoxification process with no biological activity and no potential for accumulation.
Hence, at EU level, the metabolism studies were considered sufficient to derive a residue definition for risk assessment and monitoring, based on metabolism studies in three crop groups (i.e. broccoli, maize and peanuts). An additional metabolism study in a fourth crop group, such as alfalfa is not considered necessary.

efsa_comments:
The residue definition for enforcement derived by JMPR and EU are the same (parent only).
As regards the risk assessment residue definition for the crop group relevant in the current assessment (i.e. pulses and oilseeds), the RDs for RA derived by JMPR and in the EU are different: the JMPR proposed the sum of triflumuron and M02, expressed as triflumuron and M07, assessed separately.
Comment on EU RD for risk assessment:
Considering the TRV derived for parent and metabolite, the following EU residue definition for risk assessment were considered in this assessment:
for chronic risk assessment: sum of triflumuron, M07 and M08, expressed as triflumuron;
for acute risk assessment: sum of M07 and M08, expressed as M07.
As the EU assessment does not clearly specify, whether the ARfD derived for M07 is also applicable to M08, a worst‐case assumption was taken to assume that M08 shares the same toxicological profile as M07.
For animal products the RD for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and EU are the same (parent only).

judgment_basis_ko: JMPR과 EU 모두 mefentrifluconazole이며 BAS750F는 EU에 병기된 코드이다. 해설의 추가 TDM과 동물 포합체 차이는 해당 식물 Enforcement 행과 구분한다.

JMPR: Mefentrifluconazole
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Mefentrifluconazole
Peer review (EFSA, 2018g): Mefentrifluconazole (BAS 750 F)
efsa_comments:
Plant commodities: In the primary crop metabolism studies conducted in grape, soya bean and wheat, mefentrifluconazole was the predominant compound in most of matrices (60–92% TRR) in forage (wheat, soya bean), leaf/stalk (grapevine), straw/hull/chaff (wheat, soya bean), green pod (soya bean) and grape (grapevine). In wheat grain and soya bean seed, mefentrifluconazole was present at very low levels, while TDMs (triazole metabolites, mainly triazole alanine) represented the predominant residues.
In a rotational crop metabolism study in leafy vegetables, root and tuber vegetables and cereals, mefentrifluconazole and TDM were identified as major residues, similar to the primary crops.
The ratio of R‐ and S‐enantiomers of mefentrifluconazole residues in plants remained unchanged compared with the test substance.
The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and at EU level are identical. However, in the EU, additional risk assessment residue definitions comprising the TDMs were set.
Animal commodities:
In goat matrices, parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐triazole were the predominant components of the residue. Significant change in the ratio of S:R enantiomers was revealed in most of goat matrices with proportion of the R‐enantiomer of 70–80% in cream, muscle, liver, kidney and fat. A similar shift was observed in liver and kidney of rats.
In poultry matrices, the metabolite M750F022 (and its fatty acid conjugates) is the predominant component of the residue, with parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐T also present as significant components.
Based on this data JMPR proposed the RD for enforcement as mefentrifluconazole (free and conjugated);
At EU level, the residue definition for enforcement only comprises the parent compound (without the conjugates).
EFSA considers the RD for enforcement derived by JMPR not appropriate, because
The individual conjugates are not sufficiently defined; to develop and validate enforcement methods, the individual components need to be available as analytical standards to check if the method is capable to analyse for them (e.g. efficiency of hydrolytic step to convert the conjugate to the unconjugated form).
Currently, no analytical methods are available for enforcement,
The conjugates of the parent compound are of minor relevance;
The parent compound is therefore considered to be an appropriate marker substance.
For risk assessment the JMPR and the EU RD are not comparable, as JMPR also included the conjugates of the parent compound (see discussion of RD for enforcement) and M750F022 (and its conjugates) for all animal products. As the samples of animal products derived in the feeding studies were not analysed for the conjugates, JMPR derived correction factors from the metabolism studies.

EU: Reg. 396/2005: Tetraniliprole (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
efsa_comments:
The active substance was never assessed at the EU level – residue definitions have not been proposed at the EU level.
In the plant metabolism studies involving foliar applications (apples, potato, lettuce, paddy rice), soil drench application (tomato), granular in planting hole applications (rice) and seed treatments (potato and maize), in confined rotational crop metabolism studies and in processing studies, tetraniliprole was the major component (apple, tomato, lettuce, tomato, potato) of the radioactive residue. It was noted that apart from one outdoor study in maize and another in potatoes (seed treatment in furrow), all studies were conducted indoor. However, the JMPR concluded that the indoor studies sufficiently cover outdoor uses (since photodegradation was, at the most, only a minor path of degradation of tetraniliprole in soil).
Tetraniliprole is found in all primary crop commodities and is considered suitable as a marker compound. The JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.
Metabolite tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) was the only compound identified in relevant amounts in plant matrices. This metabolite was found at up to 20% TRR in tomato, rice grain and potatoes, but generally at levels ≤ 0.01 mg eq/kg in food commodities. This occurrence was confirmed in the supervised field trials, in which it was only found occasionally above the LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg, with tetraniliprole being present at levels about an order of magnitude higher.
Tetraniliprole is not stable under baking/brewing/boiling (pH 5, 100°C, 60 min) and sterilisation (pH 6, 120°C, 20 min) conditions. Under these conditions 65–68% and 1.1–1.5% AR was recovered as parent and 27–30% AR and 94% AR as tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), respectively. Processing under heating indicated conversion of parent tetraniliprole into tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), e.g. mustard greens (up to 20% TRR), broccoli (up to 29% TRR), tomato paste (23–48% TRR) and soya bean meal (up to 81% TRR).
The JMPR concluded that tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) may occur in primary and rotational crops and that the metabolite contributes significantly to the residue in processed commodities. Hence the JMPR agreed to define a residue definition for dietary risk assessment for plant commodities as tetraniliprole and tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), expressed as tetraniliprole.
Metabolism in animals was assessed in goat and poultry studies. Tetraniliprole was a major component in all goat tissues (24–71% TRR), poultry fat (26–55% TRR) and eggs (4.2–14% TRR), but it contributes little to the overall residue in poultry muscle (3.7–10% TRR) and liver (1.6–4.2% TRR). Metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was a major compound in eggs and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg) and was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg). Parent tetraniliprole was also the major component in all cattle tissues and milk. Therefore, the JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.
In deciding which compound should be included in the residue definition for dietary risk assessment, the JMPR noted that the tetraniliprole was metabolised into numerous components, of which 17 were accounted for > 10% TRR and/or > 0.01 mg eq/kg.
The metabolites were considered in three categories, either covered by the toxicity of the parent, suitable for assessment by the TTC approach following Cramer Class III or by the TTC approach for genotoxic compounds.
Based on the assessment of metabolites, the JMPR proposed the residue definition for dietary risk assessment for animal commodities as follows: sum of tetraniliprole, tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) and tetraniliprole‐benzylalcohol (BCS‐CZ91631), expressed as tetraniliprole.
EFSA does not fully agree on the residue definition for animal products. In particular, for poultry, parent tetraniliprole seems to be not a good marker substance and therefore the residue definition for enforcement is considered not appropriate.
In addition, tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was found to be a the major compound in eggs (36% TRR, 0.030 mg eq/kg) and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg); it was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg).
In the toxicological evaluation of 2021 JMPR, this metabolite (tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone) was reported to give alerts for genotoxicity using OECD QSAR ToolBox, Version 4.5.
In 2022, JMPR compared the exposure for this metabolite with the TTC Cramer class III threshold (see below JMPR risk assessment).
It is recommended to discuss with MS whether the proposed residue definitions for poultry are acceptable. Further details should also be checked in the JMPR evaluations, e.g. whether new information was available that allows to conclude that metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone does not have genotoxicity alerts.

efsa_comments:
(a): This can be implemented by taking the maximum of the sum of compounds containing the imidazopyridine ring and hydrolysed using acid to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) or compounds containing the phenyl ring and hydrolysed to 8‐chloro‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxylic acid (IN‐QEK31) (expressed as fluazaindolizine).
The metabolism of fluazaindolizine applied either as [phenyl‐14C(U)]fluazaindolizine (Ph‐14C) or [imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐5,8a‐14C]fluazaindolizine (IP‐5,8a‐14C) in plants was assessed in the following studies: in tomatoes, indoor, planting seedling into the soil treated by soil drenching at 1.5 kg a.s./ha and 30 days later with a soil direct application at 0.5 kg a.s./ha; in soya beans, seeds sown into soil treated with a drench application at 1 kg a.s./ha; in carrots, seeds sown into treated soil after a soil application of 1.5 kg a.s./ha, and a further application was done 30 days later at 0.5 kg a.s./ha; in potatoes, indoor, seeds sown into treated soil after a soil application of 1.0 kg a.s./ha, a further application was done 30 days later at 1.0 kg a.s./ha; mature sugarcane were transplanted into treated with soil drench application of 1.0 kg a.s./ha (JMPR 2022).
In the confined rotational crop study conducted in a glasshouse, bare sandy loam soil was treated with 14C‐fluazaindolizine at the equivalent of ≈ 1.95 kg a.s./ha (0.9× maximum seasonal rate) and spinach, radish and spring wheat were sown 30, 120 and 300 days after soil application (plant‐back interval, PBI). Fluazaindolizine, IN‐F4106 and IN‐QEK31 were the major residues extracted from soil.
Regarding the residue definition for enforcement in plants, as fluazaindolizine occurs in most crops that have detectable residues a pragmatic option as analysis of other compounds involves an intensive hydrolysis step, the JMPR decided the residue definition for compliance with MRLs in plants should be fluazaindolizine.
Regarding the residue definition for risk assessment for plant commodities the JMPR considered the likely occurrence of the compounds and the toxicological properties of the candidates. Compounds considered were fluazaindolizine, IN‐REG72, IN‐A5760, INF4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐RYC33, IN‐TMQ01, IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54 and their conjugates. efsa_comments:
At EU level, the same metabolism studies (primary crops, rotational crops and livestock) were assessed as by JMPR.
Overall, EFSA proposed parent isoflucypram as the residue definition for MRL enforcement for plant and animal products.
The risk assessment, residue definitions for animal products is provisional; the residue definition for risk assessment for plant products is limited to cereals only (EFSA, 2022d). The same residue definition as in primary crops was proposed provisionally also for rotational and processed commodities.
JMPR proposed only a residue definition for enforcement as isoflucypram for plant and animal products. For risk assessment, JMPR could not derive a conclusion on the residue definition due to the lack of genotoxicity studies for two metabolites found in rotational crop studies exceeding 0.01 mg eq./kg in mature Swiss chard (i.e. M52 and M54). The dietary exposure for these two metabolites was above the TTC for compound with potential genotoxicity.
Details on metabolism studies:
Primary crops: Metabolism studies in tomatoes, wheat, soya bean and rapeseed following foliar application and on root potatoes following the postharvest treatment. Isoflucypram was the major compound in all edible parts of the crops (max 93% TRR in wheat grain, 98% TRR in tomato fruits, etc) and in cereals feed items (up to 63% TRR in straw and 55% TRR in hay). Other relevant compounds found in relative and/or absolute amount were: M01 (isoflucypram‐propanol) and M06 (isoflucypram desmethyl propanol) free and conjugates in wheat straw and hay, in soya bean forage and hay were found also the M44 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐homo GSM), M45 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐Cys‐MA), M46 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐OH), M47 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐Glyc), M48 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid – propil‐OH‐Glyc) and M58 (isoflucypram‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide) in potato tuber.
M01 and M06 free and conjugates were found in residue trials on cereals (i.e grains) at levels either comparable or higher than the parent.
Based on metabolism studies and field trials the residue definition for risk assessment at EU level was proposed as: sum of isoflucypram, M01 and its conjugates, M06 and conjugates expressed as isoflucypram limited to cereals only. For enforcement the residue definition was proposed as isoflucypram.
JMPR considered M01 could be excluded from the risk assessment based on the results from residue trials, due to the low occurrence of quantifiable residues in cereals; M06 was assess by using the TTC approach (Cramer Class III) and was found not relevant for risk assessment by JMPR.
In rotational crops, several compounds such as M49 (BCS‐CR60082), M52 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐Cys) and M54 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐GSH) occurred above 10% of TRRs, different than in primary crops. Isoflucypram was found only in wheat forage. For the metabolites M52 and M54, a potential concern for genotoxicity was identified at EU level. JMPR applied the TTC approach to assess M52 and M54, and concluded that the exposure was above the threshold for genotoxic compounds (0.0025 μg/kg bw per day).
Processing studies: Under standard hydrolysis conditions of pasteurisation, boiling/brewing/baking and sterilisation submitted during peer review isoflucypram and M01 are stable (98%). M06 degraded into M77 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol‐aldehyde) under boiling/brewing/baking up to 66% and under sterilisation up to 98%). Since for M77 a genotoxicity potential could not be excluded, in the EU peer review process, a data gap was set to address genotoxicity, since the precursor substance M06 was found in barley grain at relevant levels.
Animal metabolism studies: Isoflucypram was found in all animal tissues, in milk and eggs, liver and ruminant fat. M01 and M06 were recovered at relevant amount in almost all matrices, except M01 in milk and ruminant fat. M07 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐1,2 propandiol), M11 ((isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐carboxylic acid) and M12 isoflucypram‐carboxylic acid) were found above 10% TRRs in poultry muscle and liver. However, based on poultry feeding studies M07, these metabolites were not expected above 0.01 mg/kg. In ruminants, additional compound such as M02 (isoflucypram‐2 propanol), M19 (conjugate of M01), M20 (conjugate of M02) and M50 were found as relevant; in the EU assessment, for M50 (isoflucypram‐N‐methyl‐pyrazole carboxylic acid) the genotoxicity potential was considered not addressed.
JMPR identified the following information missing that would be desirable to derive proposals for residue definitions for plant and animal products:
Submission of cereal grain processing data for isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol (M06)
Hydrolysis of the extracts from soya bean metabolism studies
In the EU assessment, potential concerns for genotoxicity based on positive genotoxicity QSAR predictions were identified (M50, M66, M67, M77).

efsa_comments:
JMPR assessed plant metabolism studies in strawberries (foliar and soil use), peaches (foliar) lettuce (foliar) wheat (foliar and soil), rice (foliar use), peanuts (foliar). The plant metabolism studies revealed qualitative similarities in the crops investigated, with quantitative differences. JMPR considered iprodione being a sufficient marker for MRL enforcement, occurring between 25 and 98% of TRR in all raw and processed commodities. The inclusion of additional plant metabolites in the residue definition for risk assessment was considered not necessary
EFSA noted that in carrot roots, iprodione accounted for less than 10% of TRR, and therefore for root crops, the parent would not be a good marker compound
Animal products: JMPR concluded that iprodione and RP32490 represent suitable markers for enforcement in animal commodities. However, as suitable analytical methods are not available, a residue definition for enforcement purpose in animal commodities could not be derived. For risk assessment, considering the results of metabolism studies and of the toxicological assessment, JMPR proposed to include the two major metabolites found in all bovine and poultry tissues, milk and eggs (RP32490) and the major metabolite found in milk (RP36114) in the residue definition
Processed commodities: In the standard hydrolysis studies to investigate the effect of processing on the nature of residues, iprodione was found to be almost stable at conditions simulating pasteurisation, but degraded notably at conditions representative of baking, brewing, boiling and sterilisation under formation of RP 30228, RP 37176 and 3,5‐dichloroaniline

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Deltamethrin (cis‐deltamethrin)
MRL review (EFSA, 2015h): Deltamethrin (tentative)
efsa_comments:
The RMS noted that an additional residue definition for risk assessment might be established in future for all pyrethroid pesticides, which covers the common metabolites:
Sum of PBA, PBA(OH) (including their conjugates) and PBAld, using the specific health‐based guidance values derived for these compounds (EFSA PPR Panel, 2022b)
In addition, it was noted that the alpha‐R‐isomer is most probably an artefact and therefore could be taken out of the residue definition
All three mentioned isomers of deltamethrin are diastereomers and can be determined using common multi‐residue methods and instruments, involving conventional chromatographic separation. Using GC techniques, the isomers in question are typically chromatographically well separated, but according to the EURL experience, thermally promoted interconversion of isomers occurs, leading to uncertainties and bias in the quantification of the individual isomers. Still, due to the similar detection responses of the isomers, the uncertainty of the summed residue is typically acceptable. In addition, with GC methods may not be sufficiently specific to distinguish between deltamethrin and tralomethrin (see also comments on analytical methods). Using LC the problems related to thermal isomerization are circumvented
It should be noted that neither conventional GC nor conventional LC are capable of separating enantiomeric pairs. The current RD‐wordings (of both EU and JMPR) refer to single isomers disregarding the inability of conventional methods to distinguish between the above stated isomers and their respective enantiomers (this is rather a formal aspect)

efsa_comments:
Plant commodities: JMPR investigated carbosulfan metabolism in various crops, including citrus, maize, rice, sugar beet, alfalfa and soybean. Metabolic pathways involve hydrolysis to carbofuran and dibutylamine or oxidation to carbosulfan sulfone. Carbofuran further oxidises to 7‐phenol, forming 3‐hydroxy‐7‐phenol and 3‐keto‐7‐phenol. Alternatively, it becomes N‐hydroxymethyl carbofuran or 3‐hydroxy/3‐keto carbofuran. Metabolites exist in conjugated/non‐conjugated forms
Major foliar residues are carbosulfan, carbofuran and dibutylamine; soil applications yield carbofuran and 3‐hydroxy carbofuran, with phenol‐derivatives increasing. Dibutylamine declines in immature plants. Residues in mature sugar beet roots, maize/rice grain are low for identification; soybeans/maize stover contain minimal 3‐hydroxy carbofuran and phenol‐derivatives
Rotational crops: JMPR concluded that significant residues of carbosulfan metabolites are not expected in food commodities from rotational crops, but there is a potential for metabolite residues to be taken up in feed commodities.
Animal commodities: Carbosulfan undergoes rapid metabolism and excretion in animals, typically detected at very low levels (< 2% TRR). Predominant metabolites include 3‐hydroxy‐carbofuran (found in poultry muscle, milk and kidney) and dibutylamine (found in poultry muscle and liver), with carbofuran being a minor component in all matrices. In goats, the proposed metabolic pathway involves hydrolytic cleavage of the N–S bond to form dibutylamine and carbofuran, followed by the formation of carbamate derivatives or phenolic carbofuran derivatives
The EU residue definition for enforcement is more comprehensive than the one proposed by JMPR. For risk assessment the residue definitions are not compatible

efsa_comments:
EU plant
: Metabolism studies were conducted on four crop categories: cereals (rice), leafy crops (lettuce), pulses/oilseeds (cotton) and fruit crops (tomato). Each crop underwent metabolism investigations after either three foliar or three soil drench applications at 150 g/ha (except for rice, which had a single soil application at 300 g/ha). Regardless of application method, a similar metabolic profile was observed across different crop groups, with cyantraniliprole being the major component of the residues. Thus, the RDs for both enforcement and risk assessment were proposed as cyantraniliprole
Processed commodities:
Cyantraniliprole remained stable under standard hydrolysis conditions simulating pasteurisation and sterilisation but degraded under boiling conditions, leading to the formation of metabolites IN‐J9Z38 (12%–14% AR), IN‐N5M09 and IN‐F6L99 (5%–8% AR). Processing studies confirmed this degradation, with IN‐J9Z38 observed at higher levels than cyantraniliprole. Residue definitions for processed commodities were proposed as 'cyantraniliprole' for enforcement and 'sum of cyantraniliprole and IN‐J9Z39 expressed as cyantraniliprole' for risk assessment. JMPR proposed similar residue definitions in plant and processed products
EU animal:
Metabolism studies on goats and poultry using 14C‐cyantraniliprole labelled on either the cyano or pyrazole part were assessed. The majority of administered radioactivity was excreted, only limited residues were found in tissues, milk or eggs (less than 1% in poultry, 2% in goats). Besides cyantraniliprole, IN‐J9Z38, IN‐MLA84, IN‐N7B69, IN‐MYX98 were found in animal products. Based on the overall findings the RD‐RA was proposed as 'sum cyantraniliprole, IN‐J9Z38, IN‐MLA84, IN‐N7B69, expressed as cyantraniliprole'. A conversion factor of 2 (except for meat and honey) derived from feeding studies. The JMPR evaluated the same metabolism studies; in addition to the metabolites included in the EU RD, JMPR also included IN‐MYX98 into the risk assessment residue definition, as it was identified in significant amounts in metabolism studies (muscle, milk)

efsa_comments:
Plant commodities: Metabolism of cyflumetofen was investigated in fruit crops (mandarin, apple and eggplant) at EU and JMPR level (JMPR 2014). Cyflumetofen constituted the major portion of total radioactive residue (TRR), ranging from 67% to 84% TRR initially and 44%–65% TRR after 30 days on fruits, and 77%–87% TRR initially and 44%–81% TRR after 30 days on leaves. Among identified metabolites, only 2‐(trifluoromethyl) benzoic acid (metabolite B‐1) (free and conjugated), exceeded 10% TRR (up to 15% and 16% TRR, free and conjugated, respectively, in eggplant fruits), and AB‐6 at 10% TRR in eggplant leaves
The current residue definitions at EU and JMPR levels are similar
During EU MRL review, the lack of metabolism studies in leafy crops was considered acceptable only for hops, assuming that the metabolic pattern is similar to eggplant leaves at 14 PHI and field trials on hops. However, it was highlighted that a metabolism study on leafy would be desirable to confirm this assumption
Under the current evaluation, JMPR received new GAPs for hops, tea and coffee beans. As JMPR noted that no metabolism studies exist for leafy crops and pulses/oilseeds, essential for hops, tea and coffee beans uses, JMPR re‐evaluated the metabolism studies submitted in 2014. JMPR concluded that the metabolism observed in apple and mandarin tree leaves can be considered representative for tea leaves, as both are permanent woody crops. Metabolism in hops was found to be sufficiently addressed by the metabolism studies in eggplants (leaves), mandarin and apple tree leaves. For coffee beans, JMPR considered the metabolism studies in fruit being sufficiently representative, as coffee berries are categorised as fruits
Overall, the previously derived residue definitions were confirmed for the additional commodities under assessment
The approach used by JMPR to extrapolate the results of metabolism studies in fruit crops to coffee beans is not fully in line with the EU practices and with the requirements described in the FAO manual. Risk management discussion is therefore recommended to decide whether the approach is acceptable
Processed commodities: In standard hydrolysis studies, cyflumetofen was found to degrade to B‐1 (44–75% AR) and AB‐1 (32–49% AR) under boiling/brewing and sterilisation conditions
These findings suggest that the setting of a separate residue definition for processed products should be considered, as previously suggested in the MRL review (EFSA, 2021f)
Animal commodities: The RDs for enforcement derived by JMPR and at EU level are different: At EU level, it was therefore decided not to include metabolite B‐1 in the enforcement residue definition for animal products, since this metabolite is not specific for cyflumetofen (it can be also formed from flutolanil and fluopyram and any of their metabolites containing the 2‐trifluoromethylbenzyl moiety)

efsa_comments:
The same metabolism studies in plant and animal were assessed at JMPR and EU level
Primary crops: Metabolism studies were conducted on various crops such as tomatoes, wheat, soybeans, rapeseed and potatoes. Isoflucypram was the primary compound found in these crops, with significant residues in their edible parts and cereals feed items. Other relevant compounds were also identified in different crops
Residue trials on cereals showed that metabolites M01 and M06 were present at levels comparable or higher than the parent compound
The proposed residue definition for risk assessment at the EU level included the sum of isoflucypram, M01 and its conjugates, M06 and conjugates expressed as isoflucypram, limited to cereals. (N.B: The metabolic pattern was found to be different in the metabolism studies representative for different crop groups.)
For enforcement purposes, the residue definition was proposed as isoflucypram alone
JMPR also includes M01 for risk assessment considering the results from the field trials; however, JMPR found M06 not relevant for risk assessment using the TTC approach (Cramer Class III)
In rotational crops, several compounds, including M49, M52, M66 and M67, occurred at levels above 10% of TRRs, differing from primary crops. Isoflucypram was detected only in wheat forage
Concerns regarding the potential genotoxicity of metabolites M66 and M67 in wheat forage and grain led to a data gap for genotoxicity data during the peer review
JMPR proposed applying the (TTC) approach to assess M66 and M67 for genotoxicity
Additionally, M52 was found in Swiss chard at 0.015 mg/kg
Confined rotational field trials analysing isoflucypram and M49 were conducted in cereals, root and leafy crops, with isoflucypram found only in carrot tops at 0.066 mg/kg. JMPR proposed to apply the TTC approach to assess M66 and M67 for the genotoxicity. As regards the occurrence of residues in rotational crops, JMPR consider the current levels are not relevant, especially for feed items, but may need to be re‐evaluated for more critical future GAPs
Processed commodities: Isoflucypram and M01 remain stable (98%) under standard hydrolysis conditions, while M06 degrades into M77 during boiling/brewing/baking (up to 66%) and sterilisation (up to 98%)
Due to the potential genotoxicity of M77, additional genotoxicity testing is necessary, particularly because M06 was found in barley grain at significant levels
At EU level the residue definitions were proposed provisionally for processed similar to plants. JMPR also proposed a similar residue definition as for plants. JMPR concluded that M77 is not relevant for processing based on processing trials where M77 was found to be below 0.01 mg/kg
Animal commodities: Animal metabolism studies revealed the presence of isoflucypram in all animal tissues, milk, eggs, liver and ruminant fat. M01 and M06 were detected in significant amounts in most matrices, except for M01 in milk and ruminant fat. Although M07, M11 and M12 were found above 10% TRRs in poultry muscle and liver, poultry feeding studies suggested M07 levels would likely be below 0.01 mg/kg
Additional compounds like M02, M19, M20 and M50 were found in ruminants, with the genotoxic potential of M50 remaining not addressed
The EU proposed a residue definition for risk assessment including isoflucypram, M01, M19, M02, M20 and M11 expressed as isoflucypram
For enforcement, both the EU and JMPR proposed isoflucypram alone. For risk assessment besides the compounds included in the residue definition at EU level, JMPR included M12 (isoflucypram carboxylic acid) found in poultry metabolism studies at max 12% TRRs but not expected above 0.01 mg/kg (1N) from the feeding studies results

EU:
Peer review (EFSA, 2022e):
Sum of isoflucypram, M01 and its conjugates, M06 and its conjugates, expressed as isoflucypram
(RD applies only for cereals after foliar application)
The residue definition for plant products is provisional, pending toxicological data on M77, a degradation product of M06 and M66 and M67 (both metabolites observed in rotational crop studies. For these metabolites, genotoxicity potential needs to be addressed)
efsa_comments:
The same metabolism studies in plant and animal were assessed at JMPR and EU level
Primary crops: Metabolism studies were conducted on various crops such as tomatoes, wheat, soybeans, rapeseed and potatoes. Isoflucypram was the primary compound found in these crops, with significant residues in their edible parts and cereals feed items. Other relevant compounds were also identified in different crops
Residue trials on cereals showed that metabolites M01 and M06 were present at levels comparable or higher than the parent compound
The proposed residue definition for risk assessment at the EU level included the sum of isoflucypram, M01 and its conjugates, M06 and conjugates expressed as isoflucypram, limited to cereals. (N.B: The metabolic pattern was found to be different in the metabolism studies representative for different crop groups.)
For enforcement purposes, the residue definition was proposed as isoflucypram alone
JMPR also includes M01 for risk assessment considering the results from the field trials; however, JMPR found M06 not relevant for risk assessment using the TTC approach (Cramer Class III)
In rotational crops, several compounds, including M49, M52, M66 and M67, occurred at levels above 10% of TRRs, differing from primary crops. Isoflucypram was detected only in wheat forage
Concerns regarding the potential genotoxicity of metabolites M66 and M67 in wheat forage and grain led to a data gap for genotoxicity data during the peer review
JMPR proposed applying the (TTC) approach to assess M66 and M67 for genotoxicity
Additionally, M52 was found in Swiss chard at 0.015 mg/kg
Confined rotational field trials analysing isoflucypram and M49 were conducted in cereals, root and leafy crops, with isoflucypram found only in carrot tops at 0.066 mg/kg. JMPR proposed to apply the TTC approach to assess M66 and M67 for the genotoxicity. As regards the occurrence of residues in rotational crops, JMPR consider the current levels are not relevant, especially for feed items, but may need to be re‐evaluated for more critical future GAPs
Processed commodities: Isoflucypram and M01 remain stable (98%) under standard hydrolysis conditions, while M06 degrades into M77 during boiling/brewing/baking (up to 66%) and sterilisation (up to 98%)
Due to the potential genotoxicity of M77, additional genotoxicity testing is necessary, particularly because M06 was found in barley grain at significant levels
At EU level the residue definitions were proposed provisionally for processed similar to plants. JMPR also proposed a similar residue definition as for plants. JMPR concluded that M77 is not relevant for processing based on processing trials where M77 was found to be below 0.01 mg/kg
Animal commodities: Animal metabolism studies revealed the presence of isoflucypram in all animal tissues, milk, eggs, liver and ruminant fat. M01 and M06 were detected in significant amounts in most matrices, except for M01 in milk and ruminant fat. Although M07, M11 and M12 were found above 10% TRRs in poultry muscle and liver, poultry feeding studies suggested M07 levels would likely be below 0.01 mg/kg
Additional compounds like M02, M19, M20 and M50 were found in ruminants, with the genotoxic potential of M50 remaining not addressed
The EU proposed a residue definition for risk assessment including isoflucypram, M01, M19, M02, M20 and M11 expressed as isoflucypram
For enforcement, both the EU and JMPR proposed isoflucypram alone. For risk assessment besides the compounds included in the residue definition at EU level, JMPR included M12 (isoflucypram carboxylic acid) found in poultry metabolism studies at max 12% TRRs but not expected above 0.01 mg/kg (1N) from the feeding studies results

JMPR: 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
EU:
Reg. 396/2005:
1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
MRL review (EFSA, 2017c):
Root crops:
1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
Processed potato (tentative):
1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
efsa_comments:
Plants (root)
: Metabolism studies in potatoes are available, where 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene was the major component identified in the whole tuber (79–93% TRRs), in peeled potato and potato peel (57–94% TRR). Additionally, in peeled potato, metabolite M21 accounted for up to 20% TRR 30 days after the sixth application, while M23 was either not detected or in low proportions. Other minor polar compounds were detected after six applications (7–10% TRR) further identified as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthol and glycoside conjugates of metabolite M21. Based on these results, the residue for enforcement was defined as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene while for risk assessment it was defined as sum of 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene and M21 and its conjugates expressed as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
At JMPR level the same metabolism study was assessed. JMPR derived an enforcement residue definition similar to the EU, while for risk assessment a slightly different residue definition was proposed, which does not comprise the glucoside conjugates of M21. However, their contribution to the dietary exposure is expected to be insignificant
Processed commodities:
Standard hydrolysis studies to investigate 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene, M21 and M23 were not available at the EU level. However, a study simulating household processing of potatoes (boiling, frying and baking) was conducted with radiolabelled 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene and submitted under the MRL review (EFSA, 2021c)
In all samples of processed potatoes, 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene was the major compound identified (47–58% TRR), while M21 and M23 were identified at 0.5%–7.2% TRR and < 0.6%–5.6% TRR, respectively. In the MRL application (EFSA, 2023g), additional confirmation was provided for the compounds provisionally identified as glycoside conjugates of M21 and 1,4‐dimethylnaphthol during the MRL review. The same residue definitions as for plants are applicable for processed commodities
Based on the same processing study in potatoes, JMPR concluded that for dietary intake of processed commodities, the same residue definition as for unprocessed products should apply
Animal commodities:
Livestock metabolism studies were conducted with 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene. In goat study the major compound found was the conjugate of M23, accounting for 18% and 16% TRR in milk and in kidney, respectively, while the parent was rapidly absorbed and excreted. In poultry M23 (free and conjugated) was the major compound accounting up to 71% of TRRs in all matrices except fat, where the parent compound was the most predominant (94% of TRRs). 1,4‐Dimethylnaphthalene was also present in eggs and muscle at relevant amounts (29–35% TRR). The residue definitions at EU level for both, enforcement and risk assessment were defined as the sum of 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene and its metabolite M23 (free and conjugated), expressed as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
JMPR derived a slightly different residue definition for animal matrices except milk based on the same livestock metabolism studies, including the glycine conjugate of M23, while in the EU residue definition, free and conjugated M23 was included, without specifying the type of conjugate. For milk, JMPR proposed a separate residue definition
The EURLs noted that 1,4‐DMN and other DMN‐isomers may occur naturally in various plants (EFSA, 2021c). DMN isomers also occur in mineral oils (naphtha), that are commonly used in agriculture, either as adjuvants in plant protection products or even as active ingredients

The JMPR derived the following residue definitions for MRL setting and for risk assessment (STMR estimation in plants/livestock); in addition, separate residue definitions were derived for animal dietary burden calculation for folpet and phthalic acid:
◦
Folpet: for maximum residue level estimation in plant commodities.
◦
Folpet + phthalamic acid, expressed in folpet equivalents: for folpet STMR estimation.
◦
Folpet + phthalimide + phthalamic acid, expressed in folpet equivalents: for animal dietary burden calculations for folpet.
◦
Phthalic acid: for phthalic acid STMR estimation.
◦
Folpet + phthalimide + phthalamic acid + phthalic acid, expressed in folpet equivalents: for animal dietary burden calculations for phthalic acid.

efsa_comments:
The EU residue definitions for risk assessment are currently provisional. It is noted that the available metabolism studies with propiconazole (which is a racemic mixture of four stereoisomers) do not investigate the impact of plant and livestock metabolism on the isomer ratio of propiconazole.
The JMPR residue definitions (based on common moiety) appear more comprehensive. However, the genotoxicity and the general toxicity of certain metabolites (CGA118244, CGA91304 and CGA118245) identified in plant and livestock metabolism studies covered by the common moiety residue definition are not adequately addressed.

Reg. 396/2005: Buprofezin
Peer review (EFSA, 2025c): Buprofezin
efsa_comments:
EU: For plant and animal products, the default RD for MRL enforcement is applicable (i.e. parent compound only), as no EU uses/import tolerances for food commodities.
Metabolism studies in livestock were not evaluated in the recent peer review (EFSA, 2025c). In case an animal residue definition would become necessary, a re‐evaluation of the livestock metabolism studies and toxicological data on the pertinent metabolites to current standards would be required. For plant commodities, the residue definition derived in 2010 was proposed on provisional basis. In the framework of the renewal process (EFSA, 2025c), which was restricted to non‐food and non‐feed crops, data on metabolites of buprofezin that could be important for the consumer dietary risk assessment were not provided. Therefore, the residue definition for risk assessment was not established and no consumer risk assessment was finalised.
JMPR: The parent compound was considered a sufficient marker for MRL enforcement; for paddy rice, appropriate metabolism studies were not available to conclude on the appropriate residue definition (as paddy rice may take up metabolites from sediment/water systems, JMPR concluded that radio‐labelled metabolism studies on paddy rice and radio‐labelled degradation studies in water/sediment systems are needed to assess the appropriateness of the current residue definitions). The RD for RA for other plant products (except paddy rice) and for animal products is restricted to buprofezin.

EU: Etofenprox (Reg. 396/2005)
efsa_comments:
The EU risk assessment residue definition for plant is wider, includes alpha‐CO. See also the consumer risk assessment.
The residue definition for risk assessment (animal products) is tentative, because the following data were not available in the MRL review:
–
metabolism studies in ruminants and poultry performed with the parent and the metabolite alpha‐CO;
–
a fully validated method for enforcement in kidney and liver;
–
storage stability studies investigating stability of etofenprox in eggs, milk and animal tissues others than liver.
Confirmatory data were requested under Regulation (EC) No 396/2005.
The RMS informed EFSA that the requested confirmatory data were submitted and were assessed in the renewal process. According to the RMS, a new metabolism study in laying hens and lactating goat with alpha‐CO (taking into account the metabolic behaviour of alpha‐CO and the lower toxicity compared to the parent compound) will be available for the renewal process.

EU: Reg. 396/2005: Flubendiamide
efsa_comments:
Residue definitions for enforcement in plants and livestock in the EU and JMPR are comparable.
In the peer review, for the representative uses (tomatoes and pepper), the residue definition for risk assessment was set as flubendiamide, since residues of the metabolite flubendiamide‐des‐iodo was always below the LOQ in all tested samples (EFSA, 2013e). However, it was noted that the residue definition might be reconsidered, in case the use pattern is extended to crops where flubendiamide‐des‐iodo may occur at significant levels. In such case, as the toxicological data on this metabolite are limited (EFSA, 2013e), more information on its toxicological relevance would be required.
In the framework of the Art. 12 MRL review (EFSA, 2020i), considering the results of the metabolism studies, and that the metabolite flubendiamide‐des‐iodo was below the LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg in all the residue trials assessed, EFSA proposed that the residue definition for risk assessment as parent only was still appropriate for the uses assessed that included fruits and fruiting vegetables, roots and tubers, leafy vegetables, pulses and oilseeds, cereals and rice (EFSA, 2020i).

EU: Peer review (EFSA, 2019i): Pydiflumetofen
efsa_comments:
The EU approval process is still ongoing, and therefore, a final decision on the residue definitions has not yet been taken. Currently, the default residue definitions (Art. 18(1)(b)) are applicable for enforcement. The residue definitions proposed in the EFSA conclusion are comparable with the Codex residue definitions except for animal products (risk assessment). For animal products (all matrices), a provisional residue definition for risk assessment was proposed, which covers the parent compound and 2,4,6‐TCP.
Additional toxicological data for 2,4,6‐TCP requested during the peer review were submitted and assessed in 2024 by EFSA. However, the data were not sufficient to conclude on the genotoxic potential of 2,4,6‐TCP, and therefore, no definitive RD for RA for animal products could be proposed.
The EU residue definitions for primary crops were proposed to be applied also to rotational crops. Pydiflumetofen is a very persistent compound (DT50 = 8540 days EU value), the accumulation of residue and consequently the uptake from the soil cannot be disregarded (see also the general comment from the MRL assessment). The JMPR residue definition for animal products (risk assessment) for mammalian liver and kidney comprises TCP and an additional metabolite (relevant only for liver and kidney).

Additional toxicological data for 2,4,6‐TCP requested during the peer review were submitted and assessed in 2024 by EFSA. However, the data were not sufficient to conclude on the genotoxic potential of 2,4,6‐TCP, and therefore, no definitive RD for RA for animal products could be proposed.
The EU residue definitions for primary crops were proposed to be applied also to rotational crops. Pydiflumetofen is a very persistent compound (DT50 = 8540 days EU value), the accumulation of residue and consequently the uptake from the soil cannot be disregarded (see also the general comment from the MRL assessment). efsa_comments:
Plants:
At JMPR level
, four crops were investigated in primary metabolism studies: cereals (wheat (foliar) and rice (various applications)), fruits (soil) and pulses and oilseed (foliar), using labels at [PY‐], [PH‐] and [BE‐] positions. For rice, foliar flooded, water injected and dry‐seeded scenarios were investigated.
Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl was extensively metabolised across all investigated crops, with X11966341 and X11438848 identified as the major metabolites in both free and conjugated forms. These metabolites were primarily observed in plant parts used as feed items, forage with X11966341 up to 47% TRR and X11438848 up to 17% TRR. In contrast, residues in seeds and wheat grains were minor (< 0.004 mg eq/kg).
In rice grain, residues exceeded 0.01 mg eq/kg in only one scenario, showing the same metabolic pattern as other plant parts: florpyrauxifen‐benzyl (max. 6% of TRRs), X11966341 and X11438848 each < 4% of TRRs. In apple metabolism studies, no transfer of residues to the plant was observed following soil treatment.
In the EU, similar metabolism studies on rice were available during peer review. Based on those studies, the residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment were derived for cereals only. In the expression of the RA‐RD, it was provisionally assumed that X11966341 is covered by the parent toxicity. JMPR has not considered necessary a RA‐RD, while for enforcement, similar residue definition for all plant commodities was derived. However, EFSA is of the opinion that additional metabolism studies in fruits via foliar application would be needed to confirm whether the metabolic pattern is similar. Currently, no CXLs for fruits are evaluated.
Animal: Similar metabolism studies were assessed at both JMPR and EU levels in poultry and goat. Most of the radioactivity was excreted (97% of TRRs), with only minimal amount found in animal tissues. In poultry, residues were less than 0.01 mg eq/kg. In ruminants, X11966341 (up to 25% TRRs) and X11438848 (up to 45% TRRs) were recovered only in kidney and liver, while the parent compound was never detected. In other tissues, residues were < 0.01 mg eq/kg, and no further identification was performed.
Based on these findings, the residue definition for enforcement was derived in the EU as florpyrauxifen‐benzyl by default, while at the JMPR level, two metabolites were included. For risk assessment, JMPR did not consider it necessary to propose a residue definition. It is highlighted that the use assessed under EU peer review did not trigger the livestock assessment.
